title: Easter Island: The Part Nobody Can Explain

voice_performance.performance_intent: A researcher reading from notes at night, working through four files that are still open. Grave, curious, unhurried. The voice is never excited by a mystery and never amused by a claim — it is interested in both. Emphasis lands on nouns and numbers, never on adjectives: the register collapses the moment the voice sounds like it is selling. Where a claim is somebody else's, the voice slows into the attribution rather than hurrying past it, so attribution reads as care and not as a hedge.
voice_performance.energy_curve: Cold open low and close. Act 1 steady, lifting once through the excavation and dropping flat for the landing. Act 2 is the most controlled act in the film — it carries somebody else's argument at full strength and must not sneer, so it stays level through the four tests and drops hard at 'there was never a large population here to crash'. Act 3 is the driest and the most patient; the energy comes from the accumulation, not the delivery. Act 4 falls throughout and ends almost quiet. The outro lifts only on the ask.
voice_performance.pause_policy: Air is not left to the synthesiser. Every gap is written into the section text as an [air N.Ns] marker, 1.5 / 2.5 / 4.0 seconds and nothing else, and lib/script_beats.py --plan turns each one into a real gap in artifacts/narration_plan.json. 53 gaps, 112.5 seconds, one four-second gap at each act's own climax. Never pause mid-attribution: the gaps go between claims, not inside them.

provider_notes.pacing_detail: 150 wpm baseline. Drop to roughly 130 on a reveal and on every attributed claim — Diamond in act 2, Fischer in act 3, the disputed readings in act 4. Return to baseline on connective tissue.
provider_notes.word_timestamps: none returned by Kokoro — word timings come from forced alignment against this script (scripts/align_narration.py), not from transcription matched back to it
provider_notes.synthesis_granularity: one segment per beat plus the silence that follows it, as written by lib/script_beats.py --plan; 73 narrated segments across six sections
provider_notes.marker_handling: The [beat: ...] and [air N.Ns] lines live in section text because a marker in the prose is the only form that survives a rewrite. They are NOT spoken: narration_plan.json carries the clean text per segment and that is what the synthesiser reads.
provider_notes.sample_section_rationale: act2 is the most performance-sensitive section in the film. It voices an argument the film goes on to answer, and the whole act fails if the delivery carries any contempt.

sections.label: Cold open
sections.text:
[beat: exposition | awe]
The heads on Easter Island are not heads. Dig beside one and the shoulders come out of the hill, then the arms, then the hands. There is a whole statue under there.
[air 1.5s]

[beat: exposition | doubt]
That is the famous part. Here is the part that is not. Three hundred and ninety-four of them are still in the hillside they were cut from, and the largest was never finished.

[beat: reveal | tension]
And in 1864 a friar counted hundreds of inscribed wooden tablets in the houses here. Two dozen survive. None of them is on Easter Island.
[air 2.5s]

[beat: landing | quiet]
[framing] Four questions. [framing] One of them has an answer.
sections.speaker_directions: Flat and close, almost confidential. The first sentence is a statement of fact, not a tease — it must not rise at the end. Slow into 'There is a whole statue under there' and let the gap do the work. The last line is two short sentences and the second one lands.

delivery_cues.delivery_note: No greeting, no channel name, no 'in this video'. 43.2 seconds against the playbook's 46-second ceiling. The hook takes the rhythm of the channel's best-performing short — a flat concrete claim, then the turn — re-voiced for the long form; no frames and no transcript are lifted.

sections.label: Act 1 — The hillside full of unfinished statues
sections.text:
[beat: exposition | awe]
Almost every statue on the island came out of one hillside: Rano Raraku, a crater of compressed volcanic ash, worked for something like five hundred years, and the source of about ninety-five per cent of the moai anyone has ever counted.
[air 1.5s]

[beat: exposition | awe]
More than nine hundred of them are known. Nearly half never left. Three hundred and ninety-four are still visible in the quarry, in every state of completion, from a shape blocked out in the rock face to a finished figure lying on its back.
[air 1.5s]

[beat: transition | doubt]
[framing] Before any of that, there is the question everyone arrives with — and it is worth setting down properly, because it is the one question about this island that now has a good answer.

[beat: exposition | resolution]
In October of 2025 two archaeologists published a study of nine hundred and sixty-two statues. Sixty-two of them stand along the island's old roads, and those sixty-two share two features the others do not: a wide, D-shaped base, and a forward lean.
[air 1.5s]

[beat: exposition | resolution]
They built a replica to that design, about four and a third tonnes of it, and eighteen people walked it a hundred metres in forty minutes, rocking it from side to side on ropes. The roads it would have travelled are four and a half metres wide and dished in section, which is what holds a walking statue upright.
[air 2.5s]

[beat: transition | doubt]
So the question is not how the statues moved. It is why they stopped.

[beat: exposition | quiet]
The ones in the quarry stand to the neck in the slope, which is why they are photographed as heads. The soil that buried them also protected them. On a statue that has stood out in the weather, the surface is gone; on these, the carving on the back is still there.
[air 1.5s]

[beat: exposition | doubt]
In March of 2010 a team began the first authorised excavation inside the quarry since a Norwegian expedition in the mid-nineteen-fifties. Fifty-five years had passed between one dig and the next.
[air 1.5s]

[beat: reveal | awe]
They excavated two statues. Both were whole. Both were upright. One stood on a prepared pedestal; the other had been set into a deep hole in the ground. Neither had fallen over and been covered up. They had been put there, and left standing.
[air 2.5s]

[beat: landing | quiet]
They were meant to stay where they were.
[air 1.5s]

[beat: exposition | doubt]
Which raises the question of what the quarry actually was. There is an obvious answer that nobody had tested: a place where statues are made, and the unfinished ones are the ones that never got out of it.

[beat: exposition | doubt]
So they tested the dirt. The soil around the two statues carried traces of banana, taro and sweet potato, and unusually high levels of calcium and phosphorus. That is not the signature of a workshop floor. It is the signature of ground that was being farmed.
[air 1.5s]

[beat: exposition | resolution]
The team's reading is that it was both at once — the place the statues were cut, and the most productive growing ground on the island — and that cutting the rock is what fed the soil.
[air 2.5s]

[beat: exposition | awe]
For scale. The tallest statue ever raised stood almost ten metres and weighed eighty-two tonnes. The heaviest ever raised is one of fifteen standing together on a coastal platform, and it weighs eighty-six.
[air 1.5s]

[beat: exposition | awe]
The largest of all is still lying in that hillside, on its back, still joined to the rock it was cut from. It would have stood about twenty-one metres. Published estimates of its weight run from a hundred and forty-five tonnes to two hundred and seventy, which tells you how much anyone knows about it.
[air 1.5s]

[beat: landing | doubt]
Carving mostly stopped in the early seventeen hundreds. Whatever that hillside was — a workshop, a garden, a place held sacred by the statues standing in it — the work in it ended with the biggest figure still unfinished in the rock.
[air 4.0s]
sections.speaker_directions: Steady and factual through the opening figures. The walking recap is the one place in the film the voice is allowed to sound satisfied — it is reporting an answer — but it is brisk, because it is being set down and not dwelt on. 'So the question is not how the statues moved. It is why they stopped' is the hinge: slow it. The excavation reveal is four short declaratives; give each one its own stop. 'They were meant to stay where they were' is the landing — say it once, flat, and hold.

delivery_cues.energy: steady, lifting once at the excavation and flat at the landing
delivery_cues.delivery_note: The commissioned walking-statues recap is the three paragraphs from 'Before any of that' to 'holds a walking statue upright' — 134 words and 4.0s of air, 57.6 seconds against the owner's 60-second cap. It must not run long in delivery: hold it at baseline 150 wpm or faster, not at the reveal rate.

sections.label: Act 2 — A hundred and eleven people
sections.text:
[beat: exposition | quiet]
In 1877 somebody counted the people on Easter Island. There were a hundred and eleven of them. A century and a half earlier, the first European ships to arrive had estimated two to four thousand.
[air 2.5s]

[beat: transition | doubt]
There is a famous explanation for that, and it is worth hearing at full strength before anything is said against it.

[beat: exposition | tension]
The forest went for canoes, for firewood, and for moving and raising the statues. By the time Europeans arrived, twenty-one tree species and every land bird on the island were gone — among them a palm that may have been the largest in the world, fifteen metres and more.

[beat: exposition | tension]
Jared Diamond's account, in his own words, calls the island as close as we can get to a pure ecological collapse: a society that cut down its own forest and ended in an epidemic of cannibalism that left ninety per cent of the islanders dead.
[air 2.5s]

[beat: exposition | doubt]
It is a story that travelled further than almost any other piece of archaeology, because of what it was for. Easter Island is Earth writ small, he wrote. What did they say as they were cutting down the last palm tree?
[air 1.5s]

[beat: transition | doubt]
It is also a claim about the past, which means it can be tested. It has been tested four times.

[beat: exposition | doubt]
[framing] The bones first. A study in 1994 found little archaeological evidence of any collapse before Europeans arrived, and few violent deaths. A survey in 2010 found no conclusive evidence either. Work published in 2021 found steady population growth right up to 1722, never exceeding a few thousand people.
[air 1.5s]

[beat: exposition | doubt]
Then the weapons. The island is scattered with obsidian points called mata'a, long read as the arsenal of its wars. More than four hundred of them were photographed and measured for shape. They have no standardised form and rarely carry anything like a spear tip. You would cut somebody with a mata'a. You would not kill them with it.
[air 1.5s]

[beat: exposition | doubt]
Then the clock. Settlement was pushed forward from around eight hundred to around twelve hundred, which leaves far less time for a slow self-destruction — and an argument published in 2006 put the deforestation substantially on the rats that came ashore with the first canoes, eating the palm nuts and stopping the forest regrowing. That argument drew a published objection of its own, and it has never gone away.
[air 1.5s]

[beat: exposition | doubt]
Then the food. Satellite imagery in shortwave infrared was used to map the island's rock gardens, the stone-mulched plots its crops were grown in. They come to about a hundred and eighty acres. Earlier estimates, from imagery that cannot tell a garden from any other rocky ground, had run from five to twenty-one square kilometres. The implied ceiling is around three thousand people.
[air 2.5s]

[beat: reveal | tension]
And then the genomes. Fifteen ancient islanders were radiocarbon dated and their whole genomes sequenced. There is no severe bottleneck in the sixteen hundreds. The authors do not hedge it; they reject that scenario outright.
[air 2.5s]

[beat: landing | quiet]
There was never a large population here to crash.
[air 4.0s]

[beat: transition | resolution]
What did happen to the people of this island has a date on it.

[beat: exposition | tension]
In December of 1862, Peruvian slave raiders began taking them. About fifteen hundred people were seized over the following months — roughly half the island. Fourteen hundred and eight of them were shipped to Peru as indentured labour. About a dozen ever came back, and they brought smallpox with them.
[air 1.5s]

[beat: landing | quiet]
A hundred and eleven people, in 1877. That is not a parable about resources. It is a record of what was done to them.
[air 2.5s]

[beat: exposition | doubt]
And the revision has its own open questions, which the retelling leaves out. A study of ancient DNA in 2017 found no Native American ancestry in its samples at all, and concluded the mixing must have happened after European contact. The 2024 genomes date it to between twelve fifty and fourteen thirty. Two papers, seven years apart, opposite answers.
[air 1.5s]

[beat: exposition | doubt]
And in the leaf waxes of two crater cores there is a long drought beginning around fifteen fifty, running through the decline of the island's platform building — which is neither the parable nor the correction, and nobody has finished arguing about it.
[air 1.5s]
sections.speaker_directions: THE MOST PERFORMANCE-SENSITIVE SECTION IN THE FILM. Diamond's account is carried at full strength and the voice must not editorialise it — no irony, no lifted eyebrow, no slight acceleration into the cannibalism figure. Read it as though you believed it, because the audience does. Drop to roughly 130 for 'as close as we can get to a pure ecological collapse' and for the ninety per cent. The four tests are level and unhurried, one after another, no building excitement: the weight is cumulative. 'There was never a large population here to crash' is a finding, not a verdict — say it quietly, once. The 1862 paragraph is the only place in the film the voice may harden, and even there it stays low.

delivery_cues.energy: level and controlled; no lift on the tests, a hard drop at the landing
delivery_cues.delivery_note: The playbook's forbidden registers are the live risk here: sneering, the debunking register, the smug corrective tone, and credulous hype. Every one of them is a delivery failure before it is a writing failure. If the TTS sample of this section carries any contempt, the section is re-synthesised, not accepted.

sections.label: Act 3 — Twenty-six texts
sections.text:
[beat: exposition | awe]
Twenty-six lettered texts of rongorongo survive. Between them they carry more than fifteen thousand glyphs, and only about half are in good enough condition to be certain of at all.
[air 1.5s]

[beat: exposition | awe]
You read them by starting at the bottom left corner and working to the right. At the end of the line you turn the tablet a hundred and eighty degrees and read back. Every other line is upside down. It is called reverse boustrophedon.
[air 1.5s]

[beat: exposition | awe]
The longest is a chief's staff: a hundred and twenty-six centimetres of wood carrying two thousand nine hundred and twenty glyphs. It is also the only one of the texts that appears to use punctuation.
[air 1.5s]

[beat: transition | doubt]
The record of people trying to read it begins in the same year the outside world noticed it existed.

[beat: exposition | doubt]
A lay friar called Eugène Eyraud landed on the second of January, 1864, saw inscribed tablets in the houses, and left in October. He was dead of tuberculosis within four years. He had seen hundreds of them, and at the time nobody took any notice.
[air 1.5s]

[beat: exposition | doubt]
Four years after that a bishop in Tahiti, Florentin Jaussen, was given a tablet with human hair wound around it, and sent a priest back to collect the rest. The priest recovered a few. The islanders he asked could not agree on how to read them.
[air 1.5s]

[beat: exposition | doubt]
Then five years, four tablets, and one man, Metoro Tau'a Ure, said to know the inscriptions by heart. The glyph list the two of them produced has never led anybody to an understanding of the script — and a scholar going back over it later found that he had read some of the lines in the wrong direction.
[air 2.5s]

[beat: exposition | doubt]
In 1957 two Soviet scholars proposed that a short repeating sequence on one tablet has the shape of a genealogy: one sign functioning as a title, another as a patronymic marker. It is widely thought plausible. It has never been confirmed.
[air 2.5s]

[beat: transition | tension]
Then, in 1995, somebody announced that they had cracked it.

[beat: exposition | tension]
Steven Fischer's claim, at its strongest: the chief's staff is a creation chant. X copulated with Y, and there issued forth Z, over and over, with one particular glyph standing for a phallus. And about eighty-five per cent of everything that survives, on this reading, is the same formula.
[air 1.5s]

[beat: transition | doubt]
A decipherment is a claim you can take apart, and four people did.

[beat: exposition | doubt]
On the most generous possible count, sixty-three of the staff's hundred and thirteen sequences fit the pattern. The triads turn up almost nowhere else in the corpus — one damaged text and a single line of another. Statistically, the staff stands apart from every other text even when you remove the glyph the reading is built on. And the plural marker the grammar depends on does not exist in the Rapa Nui language.
[air 2.5s]

[beat: exposition | doubt]
What is actually agreed about the whole corpus amounts to three lines on one side of the tablet called Mamari. They are a lunar calendar. The argument is about where the extra nights go in a twenty-eight night month.
[air 1.5s]

[beat: reveal | doubt]
We know what that passage does. We cannot read it.
[air 4.0s]

[beat: exposition | resolution]
The best structural argument that this is writing at all is an inventory: fifty-two signs account for ninety-nine point seven per cent of the intact texts. That is syllabary-sized — the right order of magnitude for a script that records a language. The analysis behind that number was never published.
[air 1.5s]

[beat: exposition | tension]
And in February of 2024, four tablets held in a convent in Rome were radiocarbon dated. Three came back eighteenth or nineteenth century. The fourth came back fourteen ninety-three to fifteen oh nine — more than two centuries before any European set foot on the island. The wood appears to be driftwood, from a species that does not grow there.
[air 2.5s]

[beat: landing | doubt]
Which is the authors' argument: that writing was invented here, from nothing. Or it is not. Radiocarbon dates the death of a tree and not the cutting of a glyph, one tablet is one tablet, and nobody reported writing on this island before 1864 — which is why a Spanish treaty signed here in 1770, in front of the island's chiefs, is still a live hypothesis for where the idea came from.
[air 1.5s]
sections.speaker_directions: The driest act and the most patient. The opening three paragraphs are specifications — read them as specifications, with the numbers clean. The history is a sequence of people failing, and each failure gets the same even treatment: no pity for Eyraud, no mockery of Fischer. Slow into Fischer's claim and give it its full strength; the four objections that follow are four flat facts in a row, and they must not sound like a prosecution. 'We know what that passage does. We cannot read it.' is the reveal and the whole act turns on it — two sentences, a full stop between them, and then four seconds of nothing.

delivery_cues.energy: dry, accumulating; the energy is in the material and not the delivery
emphasis_words: two thousand nine hundred and twenty
delivery_cues.delivery_note: Fischer's claim is voiced at full strength and attributed by name. Attribution is not a hedge against sourcing — the claim has a ledger entry (c41) and so do all four objections. The closing paragraph must stay genuinely balanced: the independent-invention reading and the 1770 diffusion hypothesis get the same weight, because the ledger marks the question open in both directions.

sections.label: Act 4 — The egg
sections.text:
[beat: exposition | quiet]
The carving stopped. The island did not. Something else was happening on it, and it had its own buildings.

[beat: exposition | awe]
Fifty-three low stone houses at a village called Orongo, sod-covered and windowless, with doors you would have to crawl through, sitting on the rim of a crater two hundred and fifty metres above the sea. Below them the cliff drops three hundred metres into the water.
[air 1.5s]

[beat: exposition | awe]
The crater behind them is almost a mile across and holds one of only three natural bodies of fresh water anywhere on the island.
[air 1.5s]

[beat: transition | doubt]
Every spring, the following happened there.

[beat: exposition | tension]
Each man competing appointed someone else to do the swimming — a man of lesser status, who went out on a float of bundled reeds and waited on an offshore rock for the first egg of the season to be laid by a returning sooty tern.
[air 1.5s]

[beat: exposition | tension]
That rock, Motu Nui, is three point nine hectares of land. It is the summit of a mountain rising more than two kilometres from the seafloor, and the westernmost point of Chile.
[air 1.5s]

[beat: exposition | tension]
Sharks, drowning, falls from the cliff on the way back up. The record notes, without comment, that replacements were apparently easy to find.
[air 2.5s]

[beat: exposition | doubt]
And the title did not go to the swimmer. It went to the man who sent him. His clan took the exclusive right to every egg and every fledgling on those islets for a year, and he himself went into seclusion for a year, under a restriction lasting five months.
[air 2.5s]

[beat: landing | quiet]
Makemake's representative on earth, decided by somebody else's swim.
[air 1.5s]

[beat: exposition | doubt]
The entire surviving register of the institution is eighty-six names, written down by Katherine Routledge between 1913 and 1915.
[air 1.5s]

[beat: exposition | awe]
One object carries the whole change: Hoa Hakananai'a. Two and a half metres, four point two tonnes, cut from dark flow lava rather than the compressed ash everything else came from. It was found standing part-buried inside one of those houses, facing the crater.
[air 1.5s]

[beat: reveal | awe]
Its back is covered in carving that was added after the statue was finished: two birdmen facing each other, a sooty tern above them, ceremonial paddles. The statue religion on the front of the stone, and the thing that replaced it cut into the back.
[air 4.0s]

[beat: exposition | doubt]
One reading has the statue itself becoming the god. Critics dispute several of the identifications, including the shape of the beaks.
[air 1.5s]

[beat: exposition | quiet]
In November of 1868 a Royal Navy crew dug it out, dragged it down on a sledge and rafted it to their ship. It reached Plymouth the following August and went to the British Museum, where it is still. In 2018 the island's governor asked for it back. The museum offered to discuss a loan.
[air 2.5s]

[beat: exposition | doubt]
As for when the swimming stopped: three reference works give three answers. Eighteen eighty-eight. Eighteen sixty-seven. Or simply the eighteen sixties. This is an event inside the living memory of the people Routledge was recording, and we cannot date it.
[air 1.5s]

[beat: landing | quiet]
She reached the islet herself in 1914 and found two caves. One was where the swimmers had sheltered. The other had held a small statue called the Boundary of the Land — which was already in Oxford before she got there.
[air 2.5s]

[beat: landing | quiet]
Nobody can say when the last man swam out for an egg. Nobody can read the only writing this island ever produced. If the answers to either of those are anywhere, they are somewhere else.
sections.speaker_directions: The film's quietest act, and it falls throughout. The geography is described plainly — heights and distances, no awe in the voice; the frame supplies that. 'Sharks, drowning, falls from the cliff on the way back up' is a list and is read as a list. 'The record notes, without comment, that replacements were apparently easy to find' is the coldest line in the film and must be delivered without any colour at all. The reveal is the carved back of the statue; slow right down, and the four-second gap after it is the longest silence in the piece. The last three paragraphs drop to almost nothing. The final line is the question the film ends on — do not inflect it upward, do not land it like a punchline.

delivery_cues.delivery_note: The ending is an open question, not a summary. Nothing in this act recaps an earlier act; the only backward reference is the single clause 'the only writing this island ever produced', which closes the cold open's loop in six words. The last paragraph must not sound like a conclusion being announced.

outline.title: Easter Island: The Part Nobody Can Explain

beats.asserts: The heads are not heads — there is a whole statue under each one, standing upright in the hill.
That is the famous part. The part that is not: 394 statues were left unfinished in one hillside.
A friar in 1864 counted hundreds of inscribed wooden tablets in the houses. Two dozen survive and none is on the island.
Four questions about this island. One of them has an answer.

sections.hook_note: The channel's best short asks 'Easter Island statues have BODIES?'. The cold open takes that rhythm — a flat concrete claim, then the turn — and re-voices it into the long-form register. No frames are lifted and no greeting is used.

sections.label: The hillside full of unfinished statues
sections.promise: Three hundred and ninety-four statues were abandoned mid-cut in one quarry, and the ones that look like heads are standing up to their necks in it.
sections.new_information: The buried quarry statues are whole and upright — one on a prepared pedestal, one in a deep hole — and the soil around them carried banana, taro and sweet potato. The quarry was a garden.

beats.asserts: One hillside supplied about 95% of every known statue on the island, worked for roughly five hundred years.
More than nine hundred are known; nearly half never left the quarry; 394 are still visible there in every state of completion.
First, the question the audience arrived with, so it can be set down.
October 2025: 962 statues analysed, 62 of them standing along the roads, all sharing a wide D-shaped base and a forward lean.
A 4.35-tonne replica built to that design was walked a hundred metres in forty minutes by eighteen people, on roads 4.5 metres wide and concave in section.
So the question is not how they moved. It is why they stopped.
The famous heads stand to the neck in the slope, and burial protected the carving on their backs from a thousand years of weather.
In March 2010 a team began the first authorised excavation inside the quarry since Heyerdahl's expedition of 1954-55 — fifty-five years between one dig and the next.
Both statues were whole and upright. One stood on a prepared pedestal, the other was set in a deep hole. They had not fallen over and been buried; they had been put there.
They were meant to stay where they were.
The designs on the backs were linked to tattooing by the 1914 expedition; the carvings survive because the soil covered them.
The soil itself carried traces of banana, taro and sweet potato, with high calcium and phosphorus — the signature of ground that was being farmed.
The team's reading: the quarry was a carving site and the island's most productive garden at once, and the quarrying fed the soil.
Scale: the tallest ever raised stood almost ten metres at eighty-two tonnes; the heaviest, at Ahu Tongariki, is eighty-six.
The largest is still lying in the hillside. About twenty-one metres, and the published weights run from a hundred and forty-five tonnes to two hundred and seventy.
Carving mostly ceased in the early seventeen hundreds. The chisels were put down with the biggest statue a third finished, and nobody can say why.

sections.label: A hundred and eleven people
sections.promise: In 1877 there were a hundred and eleven islanders left, and the famous explanation for that is one the evidence has spent twenty years dismantling.
sections.new_information: Four independent tests against the collapse — the bones, the weapons, the chronology and the food — plus fifteen genomes with no bottleneck in them; and the documented catastrophe the parable displaced.

beats.asserts: In 1877 a count found a hundred and eleven native inhabitants.
There is a famous explanation for that number.
The forest went for canoes, for firewood, for moving and raising statues. Twenty-one tree species and every land bird were gone by the time Europeans arrived.
Diamond's own words, at full strength: as close as we can get to a pure ecological collapse, ending in an epidemic of cannibalism that left ninety per cent of the islanders dead.
Why it travelled: Easter Island is Earth writ small, and the question about what they said as they cut down the last palm.
It is a claim about the past, so it can be tested. Four times.
The bones. A 1994 study found little evidence of a pre-European collapse and few violent deaths; two later surveys found no conclusive evidence either.
The weapons. More than four hundred mata'a photographed and measured: no standardised shape, few spearlike tips. You would cut somebody with one; it would not be lethal.

The clock. Settlement moved forward to about twelve hundred, and Hunt's 2006 argument put the deforestation on introduced rats eating the palm nuts — an argument that drew its own published objection.

The food. Satellite mapping in shortwave infrared put the island's rock gardens at about a hundred and eighty acres, where earlier estimates ran from five to twenty-one square kilometres. The ceiling is about three thousand people.
And the genomes. Fifteen ancient islanders, radiocarbon dated and whole-genome sequenced, show no severe bottleneck in the sixteen hundreds. The authors reject it outright.
There was never a large population to crash.
What did happen has a date on it.

December 1862: Peruvian raiders took about fifteen hundred people, roughly half the island. Fourteen hundred and eight were shipped to Peru as indentured labour. About a dozen came back, and brought smallpox with them.
A hundred and eleven people, in 1877. That is not a parable. It is a record.

The honest gap: a 2017 study of ancient DNA found no Native American ancestry at all and put the mixing after European contact. The 2024 genomes put it between twelve fifty and fourteen thirty. Two papers, opposite answers.
And the leaf waxes in two crater cores record a long drought from about fifteen fifty, as the platform building declined — which is neither story.

sections.register_warning: This is the act that can slip into the debunking register the playbook forbids. Diamond gets his strongest form in his own words with no editorial around it, and the four tests answer him without a victory lap. Beat 12 is a landing, not a verdict on a person.

sections.label: Twenty-six texts
sections.promise: The island either invented writing or copied it, and either way nobody has read a line of it — and one radiocarbon date has just moved the whole question.
sections.new_information: The decipherment history as a sequence of tested claims, the one passage whose function is agreed and whose text still cannot be read, and the 1493-1509 date with its caveats intact.

beats.asserts: Twenty-six lettered texts, more than fifteen thousand glyphs between them, and only about half in good enough condition to be certain of.
You begin at the bottom left and read to the right, then turn the tablet a hundred and eighty degrees to read the next line. Reverse boustrophedon.
The longest is a chief's staff: a hundred and twenty-six centimetres, two thousand nine hundred and twenty glyphs, and the only text that appears to use punctuation.
The record of people trying to read it starts the year it was noticed.
Eyraud landed on the second of January 1864, saw tablets in the houses, left in October, and was dead of tuberculosis by August 1868. He had seen hundreds, and nobody took any notice.
Four years later a bishop received a tablet wound with human hair and sent a priest to collect the rest. He recovered a few, and the islanders could not agree on how to read them.

Then five years, four tablets, and one man said to know the inscriptions by heart. The glyph list they produced has never led anyone to an understanding of the script, and a later scholar found he had read some lines in the wrong direction.
In 1957 two Soviet scholars proposed that a repeating sequence on one tablet has the shape of a genealogy. Widely thought plausible. Never confirmed.
Then, in 1995, somebody said they had cracked it.

Fischer's claim at full strength: the staff is a creation chant, X copulated with Y and there issued forth Z, one glyph is a phallus, and about eighty-five per cent of everything that survives is the same formula.
A decipherment is a claim you can take apart.

On the most generous count, sixty-three of the staff's hundred and thirteen sequences fit the pattern. The triads turn up almost nowhere else. The staff stands apart from every other text even with that glyph removed. And the plural marker the reading rests on does not exist in the language.
What is agreed is three lines on one tablet: a lunar calendar, and the rule for where the extra nights go in a twenty-eight night month.
We know what that passage does. We cannot read it.
The structural argument that it is writing: fifty-two signs account for ninety-nine point seven per cent of the intact texts. That is syllabary-sized — and the analysis behind it was never published.

In 2024 four tablets in a convent in Rome were radiocarbon dated. Three came back eighteenth or nineteenth century. The fourth came back fourteen ninety-three to fifteen oh nine — two centuries before any European landed. The wood looks like driftwood from a species that does not grow there.

Radiocarbon dates the tree, not the carving, and one tablet is one tablet. Against it: no explorer reported writing before 1864, and the Spanish treaty signing of 1770 is still a live hypothesis for where the idea came from.

sections.label: The egg
sections.promise: They stopped carving, and then for about a century men swam to a rock in the open Pacific for one bird's egg — and nobody can say when that stopped either.
sections.new_information: What replaced the statue cult, how it worked, and that its whole surviving register is eighty-six names written down in 1914 — with one statue carrying both religions on opposite faces, in London since 1869.

beats.asserts: The carving stopped. Something else was happening on the same island.
Fifty-three low stone houses on the rim of a crater, two hundred and fifty metres above the sea, with a three hundred metre cliff below them.
The crater is almost a mile across and holds one of only three natural bodies of fresh water on the island.
Every spring, this happened there.
Each contestant appointed a man of lesser status who swam out on a float of bundled reeds and waited on a rock for the first sooty tern egg of the season.
The rock is three point nine hectares: the summit of a mountain that rises more than two kilometres from the seafloor, and the westernmost point of Chile.
Sharks, drowning, falls. The record notes that replacements were apparently easy to find.

The title did not go to the swimmer. It went to the man who sent him — a year's exclusive right to every egg on the islets for his clan, and for himself a year of seclusion under a five-month restriction.
The god's representative on the island, chosen by somebody else's swim.
The whole surviving register of the institution is eighty-six names, written down by Katherine Routledge between 1913 and 1915.

One object carries the change. Two and a half metres, four point two tonnes, dark flow lava rather than the usual compressed ash, found standing part-buried inside a house at the clifftop village, facing the crater.
Its back carries two facing birdmen, a sooty tern above them, ceremonial paddles — all cut into it after the statue was finished. The statue religion on the front, and what replaced it on the back.
One reading has the statue itself become the god. Critics dispute several of the identifications, including the shape of the beaks.

In November 1868 a Royal Navy crew dug it out, dragged it down on a sledge and rafted it to their ship. It reached Plymouth in August 1869. In 2018 the island's governor asked for it back, and the museum offered to discuss a loan.

The date the swimming stopped is given three ways in three reference works: eighteen eighty-eight, or eighteen sixty-seven, or simply the eighteen sixties — about something within living memory of the people Routledge was writing down.

Routledge reached the islet in 1914 and found two caves: one where the swimmers had sheltered, one that had held a small statue called the Boundary of the Land — already in Oxford before she got there.
The closing question, open and real: nobody can say when the last man swam, and nobody can read the only writing the island left. Both of those answers, if they exist, are somewhere else.

playbook_forbidden_registers: credulous hype that asserts a contested claim as settled
audit: Diamond's account is given 94 words at full strength, in his own quoted words, with no editorial frame around it and no 'of course' before it. The four tests answer it and then the act turns the same scepticism on the revision, which is what keeps it out of the debunking register.
Fischer's claim is voiced in full, named and attributed, before any objection is raised. The objections are stated as four measurements, not as a verdict on him.

Both landings that could have been victory laps — 'There was never a large population here to crash' and 'We know what that passage does. We cannot read it.' — are findings, nine and ten words long, with no adjective in either.

Every contested question is left contested in both directions: the admixture date (two papers, opposite answers), the independent invention against the 1770 diffusion hypothesis, the carved back's reading, and the date the swimming stopped.
No question-mark rhetoric, no 'but what if', no 'scientists were baffled'. The word 'mystery' does not appear in the narration.
